topics: Augmented Reality Applications; Cognitive Functions and Memory; Interactive and Immersive Displays
abstract: Event-Based Prospective Memory (EBPM) is essential for everyday functioning yet prone to failure, particularly in older adults and people with cognitive impairment. This project introduces EB-VMEM, a mobile Augmented Reality (AR) framework that uses on-device, real-time object detection to deliver contextually anchored reminders tied to physical objects. EB-VMEM's system architecture comprises three coordinated subsystems — an Object Detection Subsystem (real-time object recognition via Niantic Lightship), a Memory Subsystem (local object→task associations), and a Cue Display Subsystem (spatially anchored AR text overlays and short audio cues) — that together enable reminders to appear precisely when and where a registered object is encountered. Implemented in Unity with the Niantic Lightship SDK, the prototype emphasizes privacy through on-device inference, low cognitive load via automatic timely cues, and ecological integration by anchoring prompts in the user's real environment. Remaining work includes comprehensive user studies to measure effects on task completion, cognitive load, and acceptance, and extensions such as LLM-driven contextualization and wearable AR support. Traditional approaches to supporting PM—such as alarms, calendars, and written notes—often lack contextual specificity and may not align with the cognitive mechanisms underlying EBPM. Augmented reality (AR), by contrast, offers the potential to deliver reminders precisely when and where they are needed, leveraging real-world object recognition and spatial context to trigger intentions.

title: Deploying Large Language Models on Edge Computing Devices: Architectures, Optimization Techniques, Challenges, and Future Directions
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
keywords: large language models; edge computing; edge AI; LLM deployment; model compression; quantization; pruning; computation offloading; knowledge distillation; federated learning; peer learning; cloud-edge collaboration; small language models; edge caching; memory management; resource-constrained devices; 6G; Industrial Internet of Things; autonomous driving; intelligent transportation systems; medical applications; robotics; energy-efficient computing; distributed learning; AI ethics
topics: IoT and Edge/Fog Computing; Advanced Neural Network Applications; Topic Modeling
abstract: By providing sophisticated natural language interpretation, reasoning, and decision-making capabilities, large language models (LLMs) have transformed artificial intelligence (AI). However, many real-time and mission-critical applications cannot profit from the standard cloud-based deployment of LLMs due to concerns such high communication latency, excessive bandwidth utilization, privacy issues, and reliance on constant network connectivity. By moving AI processors closer to data sources and enabling intelligent processing directly on edge devices while lowering reaction times, boosting system autonomy, and improving privacy, integrating LLMs with Edge Intelligence (EI) gets around these restrictions. By looking at the most recent architectural frameworks, deployment techniques, and learning paradigms created for resource-constrained edge contexts, this survey offers a thorough analysis of LLM-based Edge Intelligence. To facilitate the effective deployment of LLMs across different edge infrastructures, it covers cloud-edge, edge-only, cloud-edge-client, federated learning, peer-to-peer learning, and knowledge distillation techniques. Advanced optimization strategies like model compression, quantization, pruning, computation offloading, effective memory management, edge caching, and lightweight Small Language Models (SLMs), which dramatically lower computational overhead while preserving high inference performance on resource-constrained devices, are also covered in the survey. The report highlights numerous real-world applications of LLM-powered Edge Intelligence, including software engineering, robotics, intelligent transportation systems, intelligent healthcare, autonomous driving, the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), upcoming 6G communication networks, and smart cities. The survey highlights the significance of creating transparent, moral, and reliable AI systems that adhere to new moral and legal standards. Scalable LLM deployment, effective resource use, energy-conscious computing, intelligent model adaptation, distributed learning, secure edge collaboration, and smooth interaction with future 6G and beyond communication networks are just a few of the subjects covered in the survey's conclusion. It also describes future research directions and highlights existing research shortages. Overall, because it offers a comprehensive analysis of the architectures, optimization techniques, applications, security issues, and potential future advancements of LLM-based Edge Intelligence, the paper is a useful tool for researchers, practitioners, and developers. This enables the creation of effective, safe, scalable, and reliable edge computing systems driven by AI.

title: Context Is Geometry
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
keywords: large language models; context encoding; holographic reduced representations; Hebbian learning; quantized models; catastrophic collapse; WebGPU
topics: Topic Modeling; Natural Language Processing Techniques; Advanced Neural Network Applications
abstract: AbstractThe deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) in browser-based environments faces a fundamental dichotomy: the need for user-specific adaptation versus the static nature of pre-trained weights. While quantization allows models like TinyLlama or Phi-2 to execute on client devices, they remain "read-only" artifacts, unable to learn from immediate context due to the prohibitive cost of backpropagation in WebGPU shaders. This paper proposes a paradigm shift from algebraic matrix retrieval to geometric state evolution. We introduce the Native Object Vector Architecture (N.O.V.A.), a design exploratory that projects context onto a complex spinor manifold using a "Rotation-Gating-Injection" mechanism. Drawing inspiration from Holographic Reduced Representations (HRR), N.O.V.A. encodes semantic relationships as phase differences, enabling an Online Active Inference mechanism via fast Hebbian learning. Experiments on a legacy Intel-based MacBook (2017) validate the architectural efficiency: the model demonstrates a 66× throughput increase compared to a quantized GPT-2 baseline (~47ms vs. ~3131ms per token) while maintaining a minimal 350MB memory footprint. Crucially, empirical analysis reveals the emergence of stable "Persona Vectors"—consistent behavioral modes that persist across generation steps where Transformer baselines exhibit catastrophic collapse. Code and Demos: Github

title: CPU–Vulkan Performance Characteristics of Quantized GGUF LLMs on an Android Edge Device A Mali-G710 Case Study Across Model Scale and Architecture
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

topics: Parallel Computing and Optimization Techniques; Advanced Neural Network Applications; IoT and Edge/Fog Computing
abstract: This technical note reports an empirical comparison of CPU and Vulkan GPU inference for quantized GGUF large language models on a consumer Android edge device. Measurements were performed on a OnePlus Nord 3 equipped with a MediaTek Dimensity 9000 SoC and Mali-G710 MC10 GPU, using a fixed llama.cpp revision and a Vulkan 1.1-compatible execution path. The study compares multiple model scales and architectures, including LFM2.5, Ministral 3, Granite 4.0 Micro, Qwen3.5, and the LFM2.5-8B-A1B Mixture-of-Experts model. The results show that mobile GPU inference does not automatically outperform ARM CPU inference. CPU/GPU performance varies significantly with model architecture and inference phase, particularly between prefill and autoregressive generation. The measurements also suggest that total parameter count alone is insufficient to predict CPU/GPU crossover behavior on mobile edge hardware. The note discusses implications for edge AI and physical AI systems, where heterogeneous CPU/GPU resource allocation may be more useful than unconditional preference for GPU execution.

title: A Cloud-Native Geospatial and IoT Framework for Multi-Criteria Real Estate Selection and Agricultural Risk Prediction
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
keywords: cloud-native architecture; precision agriculture; digital elevation model; NDVI; soil moisture monitoring; irrigation scheduling; evapotranspiration; flood risk; frost risk
topics: Soil and Land Suitability Analysis; Multi-Criteria Decision Making; Urban Planning and Valuation
abstract: 1. Introduction As global urbanization and the transition to renewable energy accelerate, the demand for optimal land parcels has surged. Finding viable real estate for solar farms or residential zoning is a highly constrained optimization problem. Developers must optimize for low slopes (to reduce grading costs), safe elevations (to avoid floodplains), proximity to infrastructure, and minimal disruption to high-yield agricultural soils. Concurrently, in precision agriculture, stationary metrics must be paired with dynamic micro-climate data to prevent catastrophic yield losses from unpredictable environmental events (e.g., frost snaps, sudden droughts). Existing solutions often treat spatial evaluation and IoT monitoring as separate domains. We address this gap by combining drone-survey-derived rasters with an edge-telemetry risk engine, ensuring that long-term land feasibility and immediate environmental risk management are calculated within a single unified pipeline. 2. Methodology: The Aero-Geo Framework The Aero-Geo framework is built upon two core technological pillars: 2.1 Dynamic Multi-Criteria Evaluation (MCE) The system ingests simulated high-resolution drone survey data to compute derived topological and vegetative rasters: Digital Elevation Models (DEM) & Slope: Computed using 3D topological matrices to identify critical gradient hazards. Hydrological Buffers: D8 flow accumulation algorithms calculate water distances. Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI): Assesses crop health and maps agricultural conservation zones. An MCE matrix is applied over these layers. Users can adjust parameter weights dynamically (e.g., heavily weighting low slopes for solar farms vs. infrastructure proximity for logistics) via a web interface, instantly yielding a normalized suitability raster (0.0 to 1.0). Contiguous parcels exceeding a strict suitability threshold are automatically extracted as prime candidates. 2.2 Predictive IoT Edge Telemetry & Hardware Actuation The framework ingests telemetry from physical ESP32 edge devices equipped with capacitive soil moisture sensors and DHT20 temperature/humidity modules. Soil Nodes: Track volumetric water content, soil temperature, and nitrogen levels. Meteorological Nodes: Track ambient temperature, humidity, and diurnal solar radiation. A machine learning (ML) intelligence engine continuously evaluates these streams to predict environmental anomalies: Pest Infestation Prediction: Cross-correlates DHT20 thresholds (e.g., high humidity and temperature) to predict the probability of fungal pathogens or arthropod outbreaks. Automated Irrigation & Pump Control: A persistent challenge in precision agriculture is inefficient water use and irreversible pump damage from "dry runs." The ML engine resolves this by calculating exact irrigation durations based on real-time soil moisture deficits and evapotranspiration rates. Cellular Actuation: Rather than issuing passive alerts, the framework communicates directly with cellular-enabled IoT switches via a bidirectional REST API. The system autonomously activates remote irrigation pumps when soil moisture drops critically and performs continuous electrical health checks (monitoring amperage and flow rate). If a pump registers low current alongside zero flow, it detects a "dry-run" state and triggers an immediate safety shutoff to prevent motor cavitation. 3. Extending the Framework: Addressing Fragmented Real Estate in India While topographical and environmental MCE solves physical land feasibility, applying this framework in developing economies like India introduces profound socio-legal challenges. Indian real estate is characterized by: Extreme Land Fragmentation: Parcels are extraordinarily small, scattered, and often jointly owned by multiple inheritors. Rampant Title Disputes: Legacy land records, unrecorded transactions, and active civil litigation create immense financial risk. Ground-Truth Discrepancies: Official cadastral maps frequently do not match physical ground boundaries. To solve this, we propose integrating a Hybrid Sociotechnical Legal Framework into the GIS pipeline: 3.1 Social Verification Consensus Network Top-down government land records (Bhudhawak, Bhoomi, etc.) often lag behind reality. We propose a decentralized "Social Proofing" layer: Community Validation: Leveraging local Gram Panchayats (village councils) and adjacent landowners via a mobile-first portal. Neighbors and local authorities digitally sign/attest to the physical possession and boundaries of a parcel. Reputation Scoring: Parcels gain a "Trust Score" based on the volume and historical reliability of local attestations, acting as a buffer against unrecorded inheritance disputes. 3.2 Automated Legal NLP and E-Courts Integration Physical suitability is irrelevant if a parcel is trapped in litigation. The framework would feature a legal risk ingestion layer: API Interoperability: Integrating with the Indian e-Courts system and state registration databases. Entity Resolution & NLP: Utilizing Large Language Models (LLMs) to parse unstructured court orders and First Information Reports (FIRs) matching the parcel IDs, Survey Numbers, or owner names. Litigation Heatmaps: The GIS pipeline generates a "Legal Friction" raster. A parcel may score a 0.95 in topographical suitability but receive a 0.1 in legal suitability if ongoing civil disputes (e.g., partition suits) are detected. 3.3 Aggregated Zonal MCE for Fragmented Land Since single parcels are too small for large-scale solar or logistics projects, the MCE algorithm is adapted for Cluster Aggregation. The system searches for mathematically contiguous blocks of highly suitable and legally clear micro-parcels. It calculates the "Aggregation Cost"—the friction of negotiating with N different verified owners—and outputs optimized multi-parcel acquisition polygons rather than single-parcel targets. 4. Conclusion The Aero-Geo pipeline demonstrates that integrating static GIS rasters with real-time IoT edge computing significantly de-risks physical land development and agricultural management. However, deploying such systems in complex emerging markets requires evolving beyond physical metrics. By fusing topological MCE with Social Verification and Legal NLP models, developers can programmatically navigate the chaotic, fragmented landscape of Indian real estate, unlocking previously inaccessible land for sustainable development and renewable energy infrastructure.

title: AIVA: An Agentic Intelligent Voice Assistant with Hybrid Local and LLM Processing on the ESP32-S3
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Prof.  Amey R.  Solanke; Yogeshwari Jitendra Mutyalu; Atharva Sanjay Nakod; Asmita Pramod Paraskar; Pratik Manoharrao Deshmukh
keywords: voice assistants; large language models; ESP32-S3; embedded systems; wake word detection; latency modeling; IoT device control; edge computing; conversational AI
topics: Speech and dialogue systems; Speech Recognition and Synthesis; IoT and Edge/Fog Computing
abstract: Voice assistants normally rely on cloud based processing to understand requests, which creates network dependency and response delay, while microcontroller class embedded platforms lack the memory and computing power to run a complete conversational AI locally. This paper presents the design of AIVA (Agentic Intelligent Voice Assistant), a voice assistant built around the ESP32-S3 that follows one rule: do locally what the device can handle and use a large language model (LLM) only when deeper language reasoning is required. A digital I2S microphone feeds an on device pipeline for wake word detection and intent identification. A routing layer then sends simple supported requests to a command engine for immediate device control and forwards complex natural language requests to an LLM. Replies are delivered through a speaker and an OLED status display. We describe the system architecture, operational flow, hardware and software needs, a first order latency model of the hybrid design and a structured evaluation plan covering response time, reliability, accuracy and resource usage. The architecture keeps essential functions available without internet connectivity, avoids unnecessary cloud dependence and is modular enough to extend with more IoT devices, multilingual interaction and personalized memory.

keywords: AI agent security; multi-agent systems; agentic workflows; AI-powered automation; security architecture; threat modeling; multi-agent orchestration; human-agent interaction; prompt injection; Model Context Protocol; provenance preservation; security maturity model; security validation; AI governance; trustworthy AI; NIST AI RMF; ISO/IEC 42001; EU AI Act; MITRE ATLAS; defense-in-depth

abstract: Agent Security Framework is a comprehensive, layered security framework designed to address the unique risks introduced by autonomous AI agents, agentic workflows, multi-agent systems, and AI-powered automation platforms. The framework organizes agent security into eight architectural layers spanning infrastructure, foundation models, data and memory, reasoning and planning, identity and authorization, tool and action execution, orchestration, and human-agent interaction, supported by cross-cutting governance and observability controls. The framework provides a structured methodology for identifying threats, implementing controls, validating security measures, and mapping requirements to leading industry standards and guidance, including NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF), ISO/IEC 42001, ISO/IEC 23894, the European Union AI Act, Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) AI Controls Matrix (AICM), CSA MAESTRO, OWASP Agentic Top 10, OWASP LLM Top 10, and MITRE ATLAS. Version 1.1 expands coverage of Model Context Protocol (MCP) security, computer-use and browser-based agents, multi-modal prompt injection, multi-agent orchestration risks, provenance preservation, reversibility classification, and least-agency design principles. The framework also introduces maturity models, validation methodologies, incident mappings, and practical implementation guidance intended for security engineers, AI platform teams, governance and compliance professionals, researchers, auditors, and executive leadership. This publication is intended to serve as a vendor-neutral reference architecture and control framework for designing, assessing, securing, and governing AI agent systems in both commercial and government environments. The framework emphasizes defense-in-depth, traceability of controls, measurable validation, and alignment with emerging regulatory and industry requirements for trustworthy AI systems.

title: Agentic AI and Its Applications in Data Analytics
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: Abstract Traditional data analytics pipelines rely heavily on static dashboards, predefined queries, and continuous human supervision, which limits their ability to react to fast-changing data and business conditions. This paper examines agentic AI, a class of autonomous, goal-driven, and tool-using artificial intelligence systems built on large language models (LLMs), and its emerging role in reshaping data analytics workflows. Unlike conventional generative AI, which produces a single response to a prompt, agentic systems perceive an environment, plan multi-step actions, invoke external tools such as databases and code execution environments, and reflect on outcomes before acting again. This study surveys the architectural foundations of agentic AI, including perception-planning-action loops, memory mechanisms, and multi-agent orchestration, and analyzes their application across automated data cleaning, natural-language-to-insight querying, autonomous anomaly detection, predictive and prescriptive analytics, and collaborative multi-agent reporting. Comparative analysis of prominent orchestration frameworks and illustrative industry case studies in finance and retail analytics is presented alongside a discussion of open challenges, including hallucination risk, governance, and evaluation difficulty. The findings suggest that agentic AI can substantially reduce human-in-the-loop bottlenecks in analytics while introducing new requirements for oversight and explainability. title: GUARDRAIL-CENTRIC FINE-TUNING FOR DETERMINISTIC DECISION SYSTEMS
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
keywords: large language models; inventory replenishment; supply chain management; risk communication; interpretability; audit requirements; Qwen2.5-Coder; constraint hierarchy
topics: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI); Ethics and Social Impacts of AI; Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society
abstract: The latest version 2.1:This revision adds a brief discussion examining the behavioral effects of guardrail-centric fine-tuning on executive-level reporting. Using a controlled comparison in which all data, calculations, and decision logic were held constant, the new section shows that constraining model reasoning influences not only decision correctness but also how risks and trade-offs are communicated. The addition demonstrates that guardrail-centric fine-tuning systematically moderates explanatory framing—preserving full risk disclosure while avoiding disproportionate or alarmist language—thereby improving interpretability and governance without altering underlying outcomes.This paper introduces Guardrail-Centric Fine-Tuning, a novel paradigm for safely deploying large language models (LLMs) in deterministic, constraint-heavy operational decision systems, using inventory replenishment in a distribution environment as a practical testbed. Rather than fine-tuning models on item-specific outcomes—which often leads to brittle generalization, loss of reasoning capability, and silent failures—the approach aligns a quantized Qwen2.5-Coder-14B model to approximately fifty generalized, domain-agnostic behavioral guardrails that enforce strict reasoning boundaries, constraint hierarchies, and audit requirements. Paired with a deterministic Python enforcement layer handling all numerical calculations and hard rules, this hybrid architecture separates probabilistic reasoning from exact execution, yielding stable, explainable, and auditable ordering recommendations across diverse product catalogs. Empirical results demonstrate enhanced robustness, preservation of general capabilities, and elimination of common fine-tuning pitfalls (such as trigger-target confusion or degraded states), underscoring that constraining how models reason—rather than dictating what outcomes they produce—is a more reliable strategy for enterprise-grade AI deployment in high-stakes domains like supply chain management.

title: Hardware-Adaptive Inference Orchestration: Zero-Overhead Local LLM Agents on Resource-Constrained Edge Devices
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
keywords: LLM agents; edge devices; CPU-only inference; memory fragmentation; resource-constrained devices
topics: IoT and Edge/Fog Computing; Natural Language Processing Techniques; Artificial Intelligence Applications
abstract: Autonomous AI agents typically rely on multi-turn ReAct loops that demand repeated system-prompt evaluation, persistent state tracking, and frequent tool selection. On constrained edge hardware—especially CPU-only devices with approximately 8 GB of RAM—this style of orchestration creates two compounding failure modes: memory fragmentation that eventually triggers out-of-memory (OOM) crashes, and promptevaluation latency that grows with the size of the active conversation. This paper presents FastAgent, a lightweight, headless inference orchestrator built around Longest Common Prefix (LCP) slot caching, 8-bit key-value (KV) cache quantization, grammar-constrained decoding, and an Adaptive Compute Controller. The design goal is not merely to run a smaller model locally, but to reproduce the stability characteristics of cloud-hosted agent APIs on hardware that would otherwise be too limited for sustained autonomous loops. On a baseline CPU environment, the framework reduced prompt-evaluation latency from roughly 3,500 ms to about 73 ms in steady state while eliminating OOM failures during long-running tool loops, showing that cloud-like responsiveness is achievable on local devices when runtime and memory management are co-designed.

abstract: HERALD introduces a novel hybrid architecture that enables fully local, privacy-preserving humanoid response generation on WhatsApp using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and QLoRA-based fine-tuned large language models. Unlike existing cloud-based conversational AI systems that compromise user privacy, HERALD operates entirely on-device, ensuring zero data egress while maintaining high conversational fidelity. The system’s core innovation lies in the Dual-Engine Personal Adaptation (DEPA) mechanism, which separates stylistic learning (via QLoRA fine-tuning on personal chat data) from episodic memory retrieval (via FAISS-based RAG indexing). This resolves the long-standing trade-off between style fidelity and factual recall in personal AI systems. Additionally, HERALD introduces the Conversational Context Graph (CCG), a relationship-aware modeling layer that captures per-contact communication patterns such as emoji usage, response latency, and conversational tone. The architecture integrates local LLM inference (Phi-3-mini, 3.8B), hybrid retrieval (FAISS + BM25), and WhatsApp Cloud API for real-time deployment, along with humanoid behavior simulation including typing delays and message fragmentation. A 21-day user study (n=119) demonstrates: Turing Pass Rate: 78.3% Style Fidelity (BERTScore F1): 0.871 Episodic Recall Accuracy: 91.4% Average Latency: 2.3 seconds These results establish HERALD as the first empirically validated system combining local LLMs, RAG, and relationship-aware context modeling for real-time messaging. The work contributes two reusable primitives — DEPA and CCG — for future research in personal AI, digital twins, and edge intelligence.

abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly relevant across modern industries. Businesses are exploring AI for content creation, software development, data processing, customer support, research, marketing, and workflow automation. As AI applications continue to expand, learners need more than theoretical knowledge. They need practical exposure, problem-solving abilities, and an understanding of how AI can be applied in professional environments. Generative AI and Agentic AI are two emerging areas that are contributing to this transformation. Generative AI enables systems to produce content such as text, images, code, and other outputs, while agentic AI focuses on systems capable of working through multiple steps to accomplish defined objectives. A Generative AI and Agentic AI course in Indore can provide learners with a structured environment to understand these technologies and explore their practical applications. Through instructor-led learning, exercises, projects, and experimentation, students can develop career-oriented AI skills while building a foundation for continued learning. Understanding Career-Oriented AI Learning Career-oriented learning focuses on developing knowledge and skills that can be applied beyond the classroom. In the context of artificial intelligence, this means understanding both fundamental concepts and practical applications. Instead of learning AI terminology in isolation, students can explore how AI technologies are used to address real problems. They can learn how to define a requirement, select an appropriate AI approach, create a workflow, test outputs, and improve the solution. This application-focused approach can make AI learning more relevant to professional environments. It can assist with tasks involving content generation, summarisation, brainstorming, coding, information processing, and other workflows. Students can explore concepts such as: Generative AI fundamentals Large language model concepts Prompt engineering Context and instructions AI-assisted content creation AI-powered productivity Output evaluation Practical AI applications Understanding these concepts can help learners become more comfortable working with generative AI technologies. Exploring Agentic AI and Automation Agentic AI introduces learners to AI systems that can perform multiple actions as part of a larger objective. Depending on the implementation, an agentic workflow may involve planning, information retrieval, tool use, decision-making, and task execution. Learning these concepts can help students understand how AI can move beyond simple question-and-answer interactions. For example, a workflow might receive a task, break it into smaller components, collect information, process that information, and generate a final output. Each stage can be evaluated and refined based on the requirements of the application. This provides learners with a practical perspective on AI-powered automation. Developing Prompt Engineering Skills Prompt engineering is an important practical skill for users working with generative AI systems. Clear instructions can help communicate the desired objective, context, constraints, and output format. Students can practise creating and refining prompts for different scenarios. They may learn to: Define a clear objective. Provide relevant context. Specify the expected format. Include constraints where necessary. Use examples when appropriate. Review the result. Refine the prompt based on the output. This iterative process can help learners understand how to communicate effectively with AI systems. Learning Through Practical Projects Projects are an important part of career-oriented education because they allow learners to apply multiple concepts together. A student may work on an AI assistant, research workflow, document-processing application, content-generation system, or automation project. The exact project can vary depending on the curriculum and learning objectives. The project development process can involve: Identifying a problem Defining requirements Selecting AI tools Designing a workflow Testing the solution Evaluating outputs Making improvements Documenting the project Such activities can provide useful exposure to the type of thinking required for practical AI applications. Connecting AI Skills With Business Requirements Career-oriented AI learning should also address the relationship between technology and business. AI can be applied differently across departments. Marketing teams may use AI for ideation and content workflows. Operations teams may explore process automation. Software teams may use generative AI for coding assistance. Customer-support teams may investigate AI-assisted responses. A Generative AI and Agentic AI course in Indore can help learners explore these different applications and understand how AI solutions can be connected to specific organisational requirements. This perspective encourages students to consider the problem first and the technology second. Strengthening Problem-Solving Abilities AI applications often involve challenges that do not have a single predefined answer. Learners need to identify problems, experiment with different approaches, evaluate results, and make improvements. For example, if an AI-generated response is inaccurate, the learner may need to determine whether the issue comes from insufficient context, unclear instructions, unsuitable information, or limitations of the underlying system. Working through such challenges can strengthen analytical thinking and practical problem-solving skills. Understanding AI Output Evaluation Generative AI can produce useful results, but its outputs may also contain inaccuracies or inconsistencies. Career-oriented AI learning should therefore include output evaluation. Students can learn to assess generated results based on factors such as: Accuracy Relevance Completeness Consistency Context Reliability Appropriate sourcing Learning to review AI outputs can help students use AI more responsibly in professional workflows. Building Responsible AI Awareness AI skills also require an understanding of responsible technology use. AI applications may involve sensitive information, generated content, automated decisions, and other considerations that require human oversight. A structured Generative AI and Agentic AI course in Indore can introduce learners to responsible practices such as protecting sensitive information, validating important outputs, understanding limitations, and maintaining appropriate human involvement. These practices can help students develop a more balanced approach to AI adoption. Developing Collaboration Skills Career-oriented learning is not limited to individual technical abilities. Modern AI projects can involve collaboration between people with different backgrounds. Students working on projects can practise discussing ideas, dividing responsibilities, reviewing solutions, and presenting their work. Collaborative activities can also expose learners to different approaches to AI problems. One student may focus on workflow design while another concentrates on research, testing, documentation, or presentation. Such experiences can complement technical learning. Learning With Instructor Support AI technologies can involve complex concepts, especially for beginners. Instructor-led learning can provide an opportunity to clarify doubts and receive guidance during practical activities. In a classroom environment, students can discuss concepts directly with instructors, work through exercises, and seek feedback on projects. A Generative AI and Agentic AI course in Indore can therefore combine structured instruction with practical learning to create a more guided learning journey. Creating a Portfolio Through Projects A project portfolio can help learners demonstrate how they have applied their knowledge. Instead of simply listing AI skills, students can document projects and explain the problems they addressed. A portfolio project could include: Project objective Problem statement Technologies or tools used AI workflow Implementation process Testing approach Challenges Results and improvements This documentation can help communicate practical exposure when discussing skills with employers or clients. Exploring Different AI Career Directions AI skills can be relevant across multiple professional areas. Depending on their existing education and experience, learners can explore different directions. These may include: Generative AI applications AI automation Prompt engineering AI-assisted development AI-enabled marketing Business process automation AI product support Data and analytics applications The depth and requirements of each role can vary, so learners may need additional specialised education and experience after developing foundational skills. A career-oriented approach should therefore focus on transferable concepts rather than dependence on a single application. Learning how to experiment, evaluate AI outputs, design workflows, understand AI limitations, and adapt to new tools can help learners continue developing their capabilities. title: Latent Dissonance Mapping: Deterministic Auditing for LLM Hallucinations
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: Abstract: This technical note introduces Latent Dissonance Mapping (LDM), a novel geometric approach for real-time hallucination detection in Large Language Models (LLMs). Unlike traditional methods that rely on external model verification or linguistic entropy, LDM monitors the internal inferential stability within the latent space. By analyzing the divergence between factual weights and predictive hidden states, LDM identifies "Internal Stress" preceding a hallucination. Our experiments, conducted under severe hardware constraints (NVIDIA RTX 3050 4GB), demonstrate a consistent ROC-AUC of >0.90 across various architectures, including Gemma-2B, Llama-3.2-1B, and Mistral-7B. Key Technical Contributions: Deterministic Detection: Transforms stochastic generation into a monitored process via a dynamic weighting kernel ($\Theta$). Architectural Universality: Validates that "Inferential Collapse" exhibits consistent neural signatures across varied model scales. Edge-Compute Efficiency: Proven effectiveness in low-VRAM environments, making it suitable for real-time, on-device safety layers. Note: This report outlines the mathematical framework ($\Psi, \Sigma, \Gamma$) and baseline benchmarks. Full implementation details and optimized parameters for large-scale deployments are proprietary.

title: Live Competitive Arenas as a New Paradigm for Evaluating LLM Agents: Design and Early Findings from Ante
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

topics: Artificial Intelligence Applications; Topic Modeling; Adversarial Robustness in Machine Learning
abstract: The evaluation of LLM agents remains dominated by static benchmarks, interactive environments, and human-preference arenas — none of which captures sustained autonomous operation under real economic pressure, and all static formats contaminate with no way to measure how much of a score is memorization. We present Ante (https://ante.games), a live competitive arena where third-party autonomous agents continuously compete in a constraint decoding game for real entry fees and prizes, settled through machine-native on-chain payments (x402 on Solana). The environment is decontaminating by construction: answers derive per-session from a keyed hash, and the hint corpus can be rotated at any time, invalidating memorized decoders while provably preserving difficulty. Since deployment the platform has seen 71,000+ agent registrations and 351M+ decisions; the analyzed episode corpus covers 128,000+ complete episodes from 1,154 agents and grows ∼11,000/day. We report three findings: declared model identity diverges sharply from actual usage among declaring agents; hint-bank rotations act as controlled decontamination shocks — across four rotation events, performance dropped in every decode-capable population (the top paid-track agent fell from 70% depth to 0% within an hour) and never in the population that ignores hints; and agents are not short-run profit maximizers, overspending prizes by one to two orders of magnitude at retail prices. We offer the arena’s mechanisms as reusable design patterns for live agent evaluation.

abstract: This first volume isolates and examines a conjunction that became visible in the first week of September 2026: the anticipated introduction of Apple's A20 Pro system-on-chip on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company's (TSMC) first-generation two-nanometre (N2) process, and the Apache-2.0 release, on 7 September 2026, of OpenBMB's MiniCPM5-2B, a dense approximately 2.5-billion-parameter language model trained for on-device assistants, tool use and agentic work. A professional note circulating on LinkedIn the following day treated these two events as a single industrial fact: last year's flagship, data-centre intelligence is beginning to appear in models that can be run locally and orchestrated on commodity hardware (De Witte, 2026). The paper does not treat that claim as settled. It reconstructs the concepts the claim depends upon — process-node efficiency, wafer-level multi-chip packaging, small language models (SLMs), latency predictability, true openness of weights and data, and multi-agent orchestration — and situates them in the longer movement of intelligence density from rented clusters to devices the user or institution physically controls. The argument is that the relevant unit of analysis is no longer model scale alone, but the joint production of silicon efficiency, model compression, open release and orchestration. abstract: SCHOLAR is engineered as a centralized, collaborative platform that functions as an advanced orchestration engine for academic synthesis, leveraging NLP, LLMs, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to autonomously ingest heterogeneous documents and compile an authoritative, syllabus-aligned "Perfect Note". The core system architecture consists of a mobile-optimized interface built with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, connecting to a FastAPI backend. The platform uses LangChain for AI orchestration, implementing map-reduce pipelines for semantic deduplication and hierarchical merging of content. Retrieval is managed via a hybrid network utilizing cloud-native Pinecone and on-device ObjectBox vector databases, ensuring low-latency, context-specific query answering and real-time tutoring grounded strictly in the uploaded academic materials.

title: IT WAS THERE ALWAYS

abstract: The Problem:Current memory-augmented approaches treat LLMs as black boxes, relying on text-based or vector-based workarounds that require translation mechanisms (e.g., embeddings, prompt engineering) to bridge the gap between the model’s internal state and external memory. This creates bottlenecks in speed, interpretability, and scalability, particularly for edge devices or local, private deployments. Our Solution:We propose Native Memory Layers /context layers: a dedicated, writable transformer layer appended to a frozen base model, whose weights are continuously updated during inference via a lightweight backward pass supervised by the model’s own semantic output. Because the memory layer operates in the same representational format as the base model, no translation is required—memory is stored in the model’s native language. Key Innovations: In-Path Learning: The memory layer reads, writes, and trains simultaneously during every interaction, dissolving the boundary between training and inference for memory only. Frozen Base Model: The underlying LLM remains untouched, eliminating catastrophic forgetting of world knowledge while allowing the memory layer to adapt dynamically. Computational Efficiency: Backpropagation is restricted to the memory layer, making the overhead negligible compared to full fine-tuning. Designed for consumer laptops with local modles. Portable Memory: The memory layer can be saved as a standalone file (e.g., .gguf, .pt), enabling users to attach, detach, or share memories like pluggable modules. Why It Matters: For Researchers: A novel architecture for persistent, self-improving AI that avoids the pitfalls of external memory systems. For Developers: Enables true personalization in local LLMs, with applications in coding assistants, research co-pilots, and lifelong learning agents. For Edge AI: A lightweight, hardware-agnostic solution that works on CPUs and low-RAM devices, democratizing access to stateful AI. For Ethics: User-owned memory—no cloud dependency, no third-party access, and full control over what the AI "remembers."

abstract: Most consumer AI voice assistants are delivered as native mobile or desktop applications requiring installation, account registration, and dependency on a single fixed language model controlled by the platform provider. This paper presents Jarvis, a browser-based AI voice assistant requiring no installation, built entirely with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript on the client side, paired with the Groq API for language model inference. Jarvis supports bilingual interaction in English and Malayalam, offers users a choice among multiple free large language models, and presents a science-fiction-inspired heads-up display (HUD) interface featuring an animated reactor visualization, real-time voice waveform visualization, and a scanning-line motion effect. The assistant maintains conversational memory within a session and exposes a user-supplied API key model, allowing each user to authenticate with their own free Groq API credentials rather than relying on a shared backend service.

abstract: Mit Tiny ML, Edge AI oder Efficient AI etabliert sich parallel zu LLMs ein Forschungsfeld, das auf die Entwicklung kleiner, energie- und kosteneffizienter und lokal ausführbarer Deep-Learning-Modelle abzielt. Zentral ist hier das Deployment auf Edge Devices (z.B. Mikrocontroller, Raspberrry Pi, Smartwatches etc.). Für die DH ergeben sich Vorteile primär aus der Möglichkeit der dezentralen Datenverarbeitung direkt am Erfassungsort sowie der leichteren und günstigeren Verfügbarkeit von entsprechender Hardware gegenüber HPC-Infrastruktur oder fremdgehosteten, potentiell kostenpflichtigen LLMs, z.B. in archäologischer Feldforschung, partizipativen Citizen-Science- oder Oral-History-Projekten oder im Bereich des kulturellen Erbes. Für diesen Beitrag wurden Mistral, BERT und mehrere komprimierte und quantisierte BERT-Modelle im Kontext eines Named-Entity-Recognition-Tasks miteinander verglichen. Dabei zeigte sich, dass komprimierte Modelle nur marginal an Performance verlieren, aber deutlich kleiner und schneller sind, sodass Edge Deployment vorstellbar ist. Die Performance von Mistral war in diesem Beispiel deutlich schlechter als die Performance der spezialiserten BERT-Modelle.

title: Dual-Process Neuro-Symbolic Cognitive Architecture for Zero-Token Program Synthesis via Hyperdimensional Associative Resonance
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
keywords: neuro-symbolic AI; hyperdimensional computing; program synthesis; on-device inference; associative memory; Hebbian plasticity; LLM hallucination; competitive programming; mathematical reasoning; spatial logic; domain-specific languages; SIMD acceleration; MATH-500
topics: AI-based Problem Solving and Planning; Software Engineering Research; Teaching and Learning Programming
abstract: Current foundation models (Large Language Models, LLMs) dominate automated software engineering and code generation, but they suffer from severe energy inefficiencies, recurrent token latency (2,000–10,000 ms per inference), non-deterministic hallucination, and lack of persistent lifelong memory. Biological cognitive systems, by contrast, employ a rapid, sub-conscious associative memory (System 1) to resolve familiar recurring challenges, invoking deliberate, resource-intensive deliberation (System 2) strictly when novel epistemic uncertainty is encountered. In this work, we present Oscurus, an asynchronous, dual-process neuro-symbolic cognitive architecture designed for continuous, on-device algorithmic synthesis. System 1 is anchored by a high-performance Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC / Vector Symbolic Architectures) substrate operating in D = 10,000 dimensions with native SIMD hardware acceleration (POPCNT, achieving 6.35 million bitwise operations per second). Structural algorithmic archetypes and Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) primitives are mapped into orthogonal hypervectors. When incoming problem specifications match consolidated Hebbian memory states above an adaptive certainty threshold, System 1 synthesizes and executes verified code in 5–15 ms with zero LLM tokens and zero GPU VRAM consumption. If epistemic certainty indicates high topological novelty, the system orchestrates a reflective System 2 query to a generative foundation model. Validated solutions produced by System 2 are subsequently distilled into System 1 via associative Hebbian plasticity, systematically expanding the offline zero-token boundary. Across comprehensive empirical evaluations on major competitive programming, mathematical, and inductive benchmarks: 1. Full Program & Patch Synthesis: 100.0% validation pass rate on OpenAI HumanEval (164/164) and 100.0% on modular SWE-bench Lite challenges (15/15). 2. Mathematical & Multitask Reasoning: 71.6% on GSM8K (662/924), 38.2% on MATH-500 (191/500, verified via formal symbolic algebra), and 46.4% on MMLU (210/453). 3. Zero-LLM Spatial Logic: Autonomous DSL-based synthesis on François Chollet's ARC-AGI benchmark with 100% zero-LLM reliance on solved tasks. 4. Extreme Latency & Throughput: Hardware-accelerated System 1 operations demonstrate a >200× speedup over cloud-based foundation model invocations.

title: Enterprise Content Management and Ontology-Driven AI: A Comparative Analysis and Future Integration Architecture
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
keywords: enterprise content management; ontology engineering; knowledge graphs; large language models; retrieval-augmented generation; GraphRAG; agentic AI; hybrid retrieval model; AI governance; provenance; records management; enterprise architecture
topics: Information Systems and Technology Applications; Knowledge Management and Technology; Semantic Web and Ontologies
abstract: This whitepaper examines how Enterprise Content Management (ECM), ontology engineering and knowledge graphs, and AI systems (large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, GraphRAG, and agentic AI) can be integrated rather than treated as competing technologies. ECM provides governed content: capture, classification, security, versioning, retention, audit, and disposition. Ontologies provide governed meaning: a formal model of enterprise concepts, relationships, and constraints. Knowledge graphs connect that meaning across documents, records, and business systems. AI interprets intent, retrieves evidence, reasons, and, under explicit controls, acts. The paper compares these three layers across purpose, information model, retrieval, governance, lifecycle, and operational behavior. It shows why document-only AI falls short for relational enterprise questions. It then proposes the Ontology-Augmented Enterprise Content Architecture (OAECA), which includes: a layered reference architecture with cross-cutting governance; a six-stage content-to-knowledge lifecycle (capture, understand, enrich, connect, retrieve, act); ontology design guidance for ECM across content, business, process, legal and compliance, operational, and AI domains; a hybrid, policy-aware retrieval model built on evidence selection before generation; a four-level security model (content, semantic, retrieval, and action authorization); provenance, retention, and legal-hold propagation from source records to derived knowledge; an evaluation framework, a seven-phase implementation roadmap, and a research agenda. The central design principle is separation of responsibility. Authoritative systems remain authoritative, semantic systems provide meaning, AI provides probabilistic interpretation, and agents act only within explicit governance boundaries. The paper is written for enterprise architects, records and information managers, knowledge engineers, and AI practitioners.

title: Efficient Deployment of Transformer-Based Large Language Models on Edge Computing Devices: Strategies, Challenges, Optimization Techniques, and Future Research Directions

abstract: A fast developing field of artificial intelligence research involves the nexus of edge computing, Transformer architecture, and Large Language Models (LLMs). Because of their high processing and memory needs, LLMs cannot be directly implemented on low-resource edge devices, despite their remarkable capacity to understand and produce natural language. The implementation of Transformer-based LLMs on edge computing platforms is examined in this study, with an emphasis on methods such as system-level approaches, inference optimization, model compression, and architectural improvements. The main issues with edge devices' constrained power, memory, and CPU capabilities are also covered. This work also looks at new compact LLMs and optimization techniques that increase deployment efficiency, lower computational costs, and enhance data security and privacy. A list of upcoming research challenges to enable effective, scalable, and intelligent edge-based AI applications concludes the survey.
